utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Good morning to everyone. I'll be examining you today on behalf of Mr. Mrksic's Defence. As you see, you have a monitor in front of you with the questions reflected in English. Please wait until the interpretation is done before you start your answer, thereby creating a pause between question and answer. Can you please tell us your first name, last name, personal details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Razvigor Virijevic. I was born in the village of Zecevici, Kosovska Mitrovica municipality, the republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We have some problems with the transcript. Virijevic. That's your last name, isn't it? And your place of birth, Zecevici in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't speak English, but I see that it says Razvigor Rjelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we know. Thank you. This will be corrected in due course. Will you please tell us about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to primary school in my native village, and continued my education in Sarajevo. I completed a secondary military school for the land forces. I left for Sarajevo in '83 and I completed that college in 1987. In 1973, that's when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So you left in 1973, and four years later, in 1977 you completed your education in Sarajevo, didn't you? Will you please now proceed to tell me about your education or career. Did you, perhaps, join the JNA after this?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: After completing my secondary military education, there was an assignment by default almost to Belgrade to the military police battalion, or rather any military police battalion belonging to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. That was immediately after the conclusion of your secondary education. How long did you stay in that unit for?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I started in August, August 1987. In September that same year, or rather -- my apologies. In 1977. It's my mistake. I apologise. I'm probably going through a bit of stage fright. In 1977 I was off to do a course with the military police in Pancevo. It was a six-month course. After that I was appointed squad commander of a military police platoon stationed at Avala, if that means anything. The time frame would be between February and the 1st of September, 1978. On the 1st of September, 1978, a department for anti-terrorist activities was set up within the security administration. I joined this new department on the 1st of September. Just to avoid any confusion about that department, some people say March, some people say April, the reason probably being that the decision was taken back then but this wasn't implemented before the 1st of September. That's when the department got off the ground or started working, and that is certainly the date that, for me, marks the beginning of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the anti-terrorist unit was set up on the 1st of September, 1978. Up until that time there had, in fact, existed no such unit, to your knowledge. You were one of the first people involved with this type of unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your understanding is entirely right. Up until that time, and this should be easy enough to verify, there existed no such unit, no unit known by that name and no unit with that specific composition. It was by pure coincidence that I was the very first person ever to join that unit, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one thing about the setting up of that unit. I think you explained that at the time the unit was under the JNA security administration, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I said previously that that entire military police battalion was under the security administration. Formally, and in terms of our establishment, we were part of that battalion. But all our logistics, planning, supplies, training and assignments went directly, for the most part, through the security administration. When I say "tasks and assignments", I mean the more complex ones, not the kind of thing we did on an everyday basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How long did you stay with that unit under the security administration, as you've just explained?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed with that unit until 1981, under the security administration. At this time there was the merger of that battalion, which became part of the Guards Brigade. This is after Josip Broz Tito's death, president of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's right. So for as long as he lived, you were not, in fact, a member of the guards, his personal guard. It wasn't before he died that your unit was merged with the guards unit; right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your understanding is perfectly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about how your own military career proceeded after 1981, when your unit was merged with the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In a way we remained what we might call independent, even within the guards unit. We had our own training plan, and most of our assignments were carried out independently. I can't say that we gave our own assignments. It was the commander, naturally. But the plan was our own and we would always go on our own in terms of carrying out more complex assignments, assignments that followed the logic of our very name. It was as a department that we continued to exist over there. I don't have a very good head for figures, I'm afraid, but we grew into a platoon for anti-terrorist activities. It was in the mid-'80s.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to your regular tasks, you've also referenced a number of tasks that were out of the ordinary. Did you perhaps receive such assignments through the security administration, which previously you were part of even in a formal sense?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such assignments, assignments that we received directly from the security administration. We weren't even allowed to inform our own direct superiors of such assignments. As a result, our superiors would generally not know about these assignments as we went about carrying them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say your direct superiors were not aware of such assignments, which ones do you mean, the guards unit or someone else?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, specifically I have the brigade commander and the military police battalion commander in mind. The military police battalion commander was our direct superior. He was directly in charge of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This modus operandi of your unit, did it change substantially over those ten years that you were part of that unit? So I would say between the time the guards unit was set up and Vukovar in 1991.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not substantially. There was the daily training. You know what the times were like in the SFRY. Those were peaceful times. There was no need for us to get involved, save for our regular security assignments. Whenever foreign dignitaries were visiting, we were providing escort for the federal secretary for All People's Defence and also for the chief of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the makeup of that unit, its composition? Did it comprise professional military personnel only or also soldiers doing their regular military term with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The composition, and I'm only talking about the anti-terrorist platoon - we'll get to the two companies later on - but my own unit only included officers. And literally all of them had completed at least their secondary military education. There had been a selection process, and only the best were selected. This was a professional unit if ever there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that imply that everybody had completed specialised courses for this type of activity?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is understood. Everyone was supposed to have completed a specialised military police training course, and as a result these people were, formally speaking, military policemen. I had also taken and completed an anti-sabotage course. Everyone in my unit had completed some sort of a specialised course: anti-sniper's course, a course in handling explosives, all sorts of specialised courses, whatever was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But in addition to that requirement for you to complete all of these training courses, you said that it was the best and most reliable that were selected into that unit. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. In our unit, there were no officers who had received any mark below excellent or outstanding. Whoever came to the unit with lower marks was subsequently replaced by a better student. There was zero tolerance for any excessive behaviour. Members of that unit had to be -- had to serve as a model for everyone else in terms of their behaviour, skills, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to these professional and personal qualities of those selected into that unit, do you know whether some thought was given to the ethnic composition of that unit? What was the ethnic composition of your unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you this now straight from the heart: I completed my military secondary school in Sarajevo and the ethnic background of the students was a very diverse one. The climate prevailing at that time completely ignored that feature. Nobody thought about anybody else's ethnic background. We represented a mini-Yugoslavia in terms of our composition, our unit. When the unit was made, when people were selected into that unit, the main criteria used were professional skills and abilities. But in the end it turned out that we were quite a diverse ethnic mix, except that I believe that we didn't have any Albanians in our unit. Not because anybody had anything against Albanians. I guess that those in charge of the selection process didn't find any Albanian officers fulfilling the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, about the number - I'm sure that the number oscillated over the years - but can you give us the number of how many professional officers there was?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I started answering too soon. We did not always have full strength. Normally there were nine of us plus one commander, and normally a platoon should have 30 or 31 members. I'm now not referring to logistic support but rather the members themselves, those who were trained and equipped to carry out assignments in line with the name of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you something about the unit but in relation to 1991. You must remember that year. But prior to that, I would like to ask Your Honours to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: To go back to 1991, you spoke about the multiethnic composition of the unit. I would like to know this: Since there were already problems emerging with various republics of the former Yugoslavia, did you have any officers in your unit who were of Croatian descent?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We had very capable outstanding officers. I can even give you names, if it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We had Lucic Josip, a sergeant. We had Sergeant Marinko, I can't remember his last name. There was Sergeant Franjo; again, I can't remember his last name. Then we had a warrant officer who was part of the logistics support, Ivo Pavkovic. He died in the meantime, unfortunately. In addition to him, his son also served in the unit. I can't remember his name right now, but he had also completed the secondary military school and was a member of our unit. There was also Zeljko Sinikovic, and people say that he came from a mixed marriage; his father was a Croat, his mother was a Serb. Then there was Zlatko Visitica, also a Croat. Ivica Bunjevcevic who had declared himself as Bunjevac, a member of that ethnic community. That's all that I can recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about your unit being a platoon, I think that you said that later on it became a company. Can you explain under which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In late '80s, our unit grew into a company. To tell you the truth, we, as a platoon, never really saw it as an organic part of our unit. There were, in fact, two platoons comprising soldiers who were performing their regular military service. Usually those who were more capable would be selected into that platoon. Naturally, commanders of squads were officers who had completed the secondary military school, and then there were platoon commanders and company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say in late '80s, does that mean somewhere towards 1990? Was it then that your unit grew into a company with three platoons?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can't remember the exact year, but it was towards that time, closer to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you well, your platoon, as it existed in 1981 when it was established, remained the same, except that two additional platoons were added with specially selected soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to emphasise that we were not housed in the same quarters with these people. We had special, separate training programmes and other separate programmes. So except for being one unit in name only, we had nothing else in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You have said enough about it. It's quite clear now. I'd like to now go to 1991. You must remember the events in Vukovar. You were still in Belgrade at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It's been a long time. Normally when I speak of Vukovar I feel I must give the history of events preceding Vukovar; otherwise, I feel the story's incomplete. But, yes, I was in Belgrade during the Vukovar events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we turn to that subject of your service in Vukovar and that of your company, let us clarify this: Will you agree with me that in 1990 and 1991 things started happening in the former Yugoslavia? Did you and members of your unit take part in some tasks preceding Vukovar, something that was quite atypical and outside of Belgrade where your headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I told you that I can't separate 1991 and Vukovar from the events that preceded it. I'm now referring to 1990 specifically. I, and everybody else who had learned of some events, were shocked. I don't know what other word to use to describe our shock. I remember very well that on the 29th of November - I don't know whether the Trial Chamber knows that that was the day of the republic, the state holiday - on that day I was invited to come to the command headquarters of the Guards Brigade. It was my day off. I was at home. And I was summoned to come in civilian clothes, which is what I did. When I arrived at the headquarters, I went to the duty operations officer. You can verify based on the duty logbook who was on duty on that day. So when I arrived there, I found three of my fellow soldiers who were there: Ramadan Huric, Dragan Djorovic, and Radomir Vucinic. I think that later on I learned that many of us had been summoned but the four of us were the first to arrive. We received an order from the duty operations officer of the Guards Brigade to go to Zagreb. We were given a car. I think it was an Opel Record but I'm not sure. It was a passenger car at any rate. We were told to take equipment that we required, and naturally that implied weapons, to put it into the trunk and to go to Zagreb as soon as possible. We had a radio in the car. Since I was the most senior in the group, I was considered a leader. We were told to establish radio communication. I'm not sure what the signal code was, but we were to report to the duty officer of the military police of the 5th Military District. Once again, we were told if we received a response, and there was again a code, that we were to continue to Varazdin. Something else: We used military insignia on our vehicle, because soldiers had been harassed in Croatia already and it was safer to display these all the same, just because the Zagreb police wouldn't think to stop us. And that's what we did. So the first response we got was to be off to Varazdin immediately, so we did. A second time around I got another code telling me to drive by the military district command in Zagreb, which is what I eventually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we begin, needless to say, I would like to ask you to please put in the briefest possible terms what the objective was of that mission. First of all, I would like to ask you: Do you know under whose orders you were acting here?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't know for as long as we were still on the road. When I arrived at the 5th Military District headquarters I finally found out. We had General Aca Vasiljevic waiting for us there. At the time he was chief of the security administration. He received us on the premises of the counter-intelligence group. The abbreviation used is KOG. There were four of us. There was a brief interview, a conversation, and he informed us that people in Croatia had begun to arm themselves. He said we were there to perform some assignments, operative ones, and try to arrest those who had received weapons and bring them in to stand trial. In order to be able to recognise such persons, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic showed us some footage that was later shown on Radio-Television Serbia. This was all going on on the 29th [Realtime transcript read in error "20th"] of November. And this footage was shown on the T.V. on the 20th of January, I believe. No one had known about this at this point, but this footage helped us show the players, so we at least knew the people we were to arrest and take in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we continue, there's something about the transcript. You gave us the date when you were shown this footage. If you can please repeat because I think there's an error here in terms of the date. When were you shown these parts of footage?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 29th, that very day, the day we arrived in Zagreb, the day of the republic, Dan Republike day in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. There was an error. It said the 20th, whereas you said the 29th. Just another thing, just to make sure I understand you correctly, General Vasiljevic was waiting for you right there and he was the head at the time of the JNA's security administration; right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he specified that this was absolutely classified information, not to be shared with anyone including our own commander. Being soldiers we understood exactly what he was driving at. We spent the night in Zagreb and we were given a vehicle the next day, as well as a driver. But I'm not sure about the latter. Yes, there was a driver we were assigned, but I didn't know his name because I didn't know anyone around there. So this driver took us to Virovitica, the reason being the persons discussed earlier hailed from that area or rather that town?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember their names, the people you were supposed to arrest?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Djuro Decak; he was occupying a post with the local HDZ in Virovitica municipality. There was someone else, Habijanec. I think he was the president of Virovitica's municipal assembly. Unfortunately these were two JNA NCOs. But I realised later on that they hadn't completed their secondary military schooling. To all of us who had completed such training, this spelled trouble, because such people were capable of committing -- of doing silly things. And there was another person called Franjo Horvat, who was also supposed to be arrested, as well as a man named Vlado, whose last name I can't remember right now. Another important thing is Djuro Decak and Habijanec were based in Virovitica, whereas Vlado Sabaric was in Koprivnica. He was a checkpoint commander, this border patrol commander. There was this video showing him in conversation with Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we continue, speaking of this footage, this video, you saw parts of it, but in January it was shown to the general public throughout the former Yugoslavia, the portion that you had been shown as well as other things that you saw in that video.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was shown in its entirety sometime in January. We had only seen brief portions of that footage just in order to see these people's faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We're talking about January.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: January '92. Oh, I'm sorry, January '91?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, what was that video about, just to set the transcript right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, January '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In the briefest possible terms this video was shown to the general public in January 1991. What was this about? You mentioned a man named Spegelj. In the briefest possible terms, tell us what the video was about.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: During the arrest we were actually on the ground, right there. This video was released for public viewing. There had been an attempt at arresting these people back in '90, and I'm not sure why it was failed. Then we were back in Belgrade and it was January. But we hadn't spent all this time in Croatia, if that's what you mean, if that's of any interest to you. In 1991, after the arrests were made, we heard from General Vasiljevic that this had been shown, but we weren't given a chance to see it in Croatia. Back then I didn't even know what it was about. Believe me, it wasn't before I returned to Belgrade the concern and shock that this had caused in my own environment, with people all around me. I think the Chamber already knows because this has been shown so many times. It was about people arming themselves; it was about people being killed. Whenever Spegelj was mentioning the dumdum bullets, the stores -- but to be quite frank I didn't see that because I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we go on to that, I would like to go back to one of your previous answers. General Vasiljevic had told you what your assignment was, and that this was classified information that you weren't to share even with your own commander. Which commander did he have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: At the time the commander of my Guards Brigade was Mile Mrksic, the then colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly how long this assignment took before you were able to return to Belgrade? Because let me get this straight: It seems you were off a number of different times. Can you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first time we were off was on the 29th of November, 1990, the four of us went, and then after that the entire group went without the commander because the commander was off on mission. So what happened was it was down to me to organise these arrests. Let me say, though, that Aca Vasiljevic told us that everything had to be done in keeping with the law; that not even the least amount of force was to be used, because these were essential witnesses, essential for him to be able to prove that the arming process had begun in Croatia. The first attempted arrest occurred in early December 1990. The four of us spent about four days in the area, observing, just looking, seeing who was where and what the best way to do this was. And then the remainder of the unit arrived. They arrived in Zagreb in Puch vehicles. The next day, and don't hold me to the date, but it may have been around the 3rd or the 4th of December, around that time, we organised the arrest of this group. We went to Zagreb and then left Zagreb to go and arrest these persons early in December, as I said. So the whole hog, the forensic officer, the black Meraja, the paddy wagon that we used. I have a sound in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, please, you completed this mission eventually, didn't you, and the persons you mentioned were arrested?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Back in 1990, when we were off, somebody stopped this mission just before the arrest was made. We arrived in Virovitica, all of us, and then we were radioed to go straight to the barracks. We waited until midnight. Aca Vasiljevic was not with us; that's one thing you have to know. I think it was Colonel Gligorevic who was with us. And we waited and waited, biding our time. And then after midnight we were told to drive back to Zagreb because no arrest would be made. Later when we talked to Aca, we once asked him what was the problem with that, and he said the federal secretary was out of the time at the time and there was no one to approve the mission, to tell him to go ahead with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the federal secretary was in?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In Hungary. That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who was the federal secretary at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These people were eventually arrested. When was this and who did it?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The first mission that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did go back to Belgrade several times, and then in January 1991 we returned to the area and arrested the persons specified above. I really have a problem with dates, you see. It's January. You might be about the 20th, give or take a day or two, when this movie was shown. They were arrested on the day the film was shown on RTS, Radio-Television Serbia. And there are documents that show that. It should be easy enough to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talked about these people you mentioned the HDZ in reference to some of them. What were you told at the time about these persons and about the involvement of the HDZ in the arming process in Croatia, in the arming campaign?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a low-ranking officer so I wasn't told much, but what I knew about the HDZ is that they were a nationalist party; they were driving -- they were pushing for a breakup of Yugoslavia. And it was with that sort of intentions that they started covertly importing weapons from Hungary. That's what I knew about it. Later on the ground I, indeed, reassured myself that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say in your conversation with Atso, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean General Atso Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The second time you went to Croatia, same orders, same remit, was that done the same way as the first time around?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But one thing I have to say, the equipment we brought the first time around, we arrived in our vehicle with our vehicle and we left this behind in Zagreb in the barracks. So we found it when we got back, but we flew back to Zagreb. The second time around we went to Croatia, we flew by plane pursuant to orders from the chief of the security administration General Atso Vasiljevic. Nobody in the barracks itself, even the commander, knew what we were up to, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, your commander wasn't aware of your exact remit or his officers, officers from the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no one in the Guards Brigade knew what we were up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you go in military uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The second time around it was in plain clothes that we went. We landed at Crkaja Op Krka [phoen], and we drove in a van with civilian registration plates to Gajova street. I think that's where the military remand prison used to be in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about Spegelj. For the benefit of the Chamber, can you explain who that person was?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 5th Military District. I can't give you the exact year, but it was certainly in the late '80s. And I think it was in this capacity that he eventually required, the commander of the 5th Military District. So he was a JNA general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time when the film was shot, when you were on this mission and when you saw these people on the film footage, was he still then an active-duty JNA general?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that he had already retired at the time, but he was appointed the minister of the army, or something to that effect, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did your mission then conclude, what you were doing there?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. We went for the third time. At the insistence of Atso Vasiljevic we went for the third time. Once again nobody in our barracks knew about this. We were supposed to capture people from whose houses the weapons were distributed. We were told that they were distributed to the HDZ members, but I can't be fully certain about this. We were to arrest Belanija from Suho Polje. I can't remember his first name. Prior to this, the Croatian police also attempted to arrest Belanija. This was the time when they were in gaol, for the sake of the court proceedings. I know that they failed in this arrest attempt, so we were given this assignment, but we didn't find him at the specified address so we didn't arrest him either. However, we managed to arrest -- I remember quite a few details because, to me, this all resembled a bad movie. I couldn't believe that something like this could be going on in my country. We arrested Mehmed Zeljko from the village of Zubica in Podravska Slatina municipality. I remember that I provided security to the people arresting him, and he was arrested by General Atso Vasiljevic and my commander specifically. In order to stay within the bounds of the law, we brought in a forensic technician. The weapons were found on the premises. And initially he confessed about everything and later on, in court, he denied it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea about the date?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: February of '91, or maybe March. I know that we had another arrest, Bijelobrk Vinko, who was selling bananas on the market, was also implicated, and we arrested him, took him to gaol. And then it was out of our hands. Somebody else took him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now turn to your unit, your brigade, just before they were deployed to Vukovar. Do you remember that period of time?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Who wouldn't? Of course I remember how we went to Vukovar. I remember that well. We knew about the events that preceded Vukovar. We were -- we were informed from the media. Perhaps it was exaggerated, the reportings, but we knew there was a war going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your platoon go, or perhaps the entire company, with the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We arrived at the same time, but my particular unit, the anti-terrorist platoon, went out before. We were billeted in the vicinity of Sid and we were told that we were to provide flank security to the brigade during the march.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you had set out earlier in order to secure the march of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the way up to Negoslavci. However, we didn't really implement our assignment, because when we arrived there we were told that we should join and mingle with the brigade, and that's how we went to Negoslavci. A person was wounded just before we entered Negoslavci, I think in Djelatovci village. This fellow wasn't in my unit but rather a member of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since we already know that the Guards Brigade had its command headquarters in Negoslavci, please tell us, did your unit stay in Negoslavci or move on to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: On that day when we arrived, all of us stayed in Negoslavci. As far as I remember, and I'm not fully certain about this, our unit stayed there, but a part of the brigade moved on to Vukovar. I'm not certain about the time. It wasn't on that day or on the following. I think it was on the third day that they moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From that time on, until the fall of Vukovar, were you personally in Vukovar with your unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander was in charge of our unit. No, it wasn't from that day. No. We were introduced a day later, a day later, after the brigade entered Vukovar. So from that day on I was in Vukovar directly on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember during that stay whether there were any journalists in your unit, staying with your unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. The only single journalist who was with us was the journalist of SkyNews. I think his name was Van Lynden. There was also an interpreter who had a local last name, shortish, blonde man, I think, and there was a cameraman. So I think those three were the only ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the SkyNews crew was there, comprising cameraman, interpreter, and this journalist that you described.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. In fact, there is some footage where I was recorded. I have it at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how long they stayed with your unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The positions of my unit were such that my squad, which was the first squad, was in the first house and they were in the house with the commander. And I think that they stayed with us for a day or two. In fact, when we went into combat to pierce some enemy lines, they went with us. And they taped it on video, and that was broadcast on the main news programme. The footage shows people running, taking shelter from the fire, and so on. There's some footage of Mr. Van Lynden and my commander too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't remember seeing any other journalists. You didn't have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody really was looking forward to going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go into private session briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Virijevic, I'm now going to turn to a completely different topic. I'm not going to go into other aspects of your war experience at Vukovar. I'm specifically interested in the day Vukovar fell. Can you describe to me what you did on that day, you and other people around you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that day above all other days in Vukovar and how not to remember it. It was the day war ended. No more killings; no more enemy side. I remember that day, perhaps not all of the details, but I have quite a good idea of the sequence of events on that day because I was so overjoyed that the war was over. I remember it as something positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what you remember? Let's start with the morning hours. Was there any combat in the morning? Did you participate in any of it? And what was taking place that morning?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the axis held by my unit, there was no combat whatsoever. We were housed in Pavle's house. That's what it was called. Pavle was a private entrepreneur before the war in Vukovar. He was a wealthy man. Everybody knew his house; that's why it was called Pavle's house. So we left the house towards the Ruthenian church, and then further on towards the fire house. There was no resistance whatsoever. When we reached the fire house, we heard the order of Colonel Panic to halt, and that the negotiations were in progress and that it seemed as though Vukovar would surrender. We complied with the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we continue, you mentioned Colonel Panic. Which one do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Panic, head -- chief of staff of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he a colonel then? That's my follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you're sure that he was chief of staff of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm positive about that. Miodrag Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What were you told, then, when you received that order on the radio, other than to halt?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We were told to wait as negotiations were in progress, and it seemed as though there would be a surrender. So we waited. And then, since I was standing close to the commander, I heard on the radio that we were given the green light to move on. We were to proceed carefully and sweep the terrain to ensure that there were no pockets of resistance remaining anywhere. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that the case? Was there no pockets of resistance anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was no resistance at all. I remember that we were moving through the area where the school is, and then I'm not sure what these neighbourhoods are called, and we were calling, issuing calls to the residents to come out from the shelters. We were telling them, the army is there; it's safe. People were leaving shelters. We were moving on. And we were directing people to go to Velepromet as that was the gathering site. People were asking us questions, and we used to tell them, Well, just go there, and then following that you will be able to go home. That was our understanding. So we were moving on, and then we went to a small elevation and entered the high school. And we could tell that the high school had been used by the military, it was used for military purposes. We found some food there and some other military equipment. Especially the gym was heavily used and there were many anti-tank mines in one part of the building. Since I had completed my civil protection training, the thought that crossed my mind was, thank god that nobody had activated these mines, because they would have inflicted severe damage. And then we proceeded on towards the Catholic church, which was already on fire, its roof was. We entered the church and found the priest there with nuns. They came out to greet us. I spoke to the priest, I apologised. I still remember what I said to him. I'm slightly religious myself, but I know this is a house of god. There's a war on. Let's just have a look to see if any soldiers were here. He said, "No problem at all. No soldiers were ever here. You can have a look if you like." So we searched it. We didn't really search it properly, but we realised that no traces of any soldiers present were there. And he probably didn't expect us to be that respectful, and he wanted to have a certificate signed to the effect that we had been there so that no one else would search the church, if anyone else came around, the church or search him or the nuns. Mladen Maric was with us but he wasn't in command, the commander was. He signed the certificate on our behalf that such and such a unit had searched the premises, that nothing needed doing from there on. So we just left and proceeded. I remember something happening -- well, it's a war, you know. Soldiers were dying. But we found this accordion and nobody cared about the war any longer. There was this accordion and we used it to set up a dance. We were singing this song, Danube, Danube, it was the end of Vukovar, with Vukovar being conquered, and all of that. So we reached Mitnica in the end. It's not much of a distance, really. I can't remember right now. But it's nearby. Well, Mitnica, there you have it. We started calling on the people there to come out slowly. There was no reason or anything, and right there that day is where it ended. I don't think you could call it a war operation, but at least our involvement in the war, that's where it ended and that's where the war in Vukovar ended for me personally. After that the only thing left were a number of technicalities, going back, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said you went to Mitnica. Did you reach the water tower in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we reached the water tower itself, and I think we went through the first three or four rows of the houses behind the water tower, but not further than that. We went as far as -- there's a detail there. It's not really important, but it just regaled my heart. This man came forward. He wasn't armed. He surrendered. And we just sent him off in a column. I think I remember his name, Hrvoje Dzalto. I think he ended up in Zagreb. You see what I mean? I think I asked questions later on. He left but I don't think he was harmed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you say the only person who came forward and surrendered in uniform bearing arms until you disarmed him. That's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That really appealed to me because he came forward wearing a full uniform, helmet, armed. That was an honourable act in my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see anybody else surrendering as soldiers in their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't along that axis. I was over in that other area, Mitnica, where all the people were coming. The elderly, women, children, some middle-aged children, they were being evacuated in the direction of Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: About the water tower, did you notice at the time if anything was going on on the water tower itself?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was something about who should be the first to hoist the flag on the water tower, our guys. And the meaning was that person was the first to liberate Vukovar, a symbol of something or other, the end of something or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anyone end up hoisting that flag?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was that unit. We didn't much feel like climbing ourselves. It was commander Zunic. That unit, he was probably the first to climb up and put the flag on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember whose flag that was?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The flag, we were all -- the Yugoslav flag. What else could it possibly have been. You know the times back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The Yugoslav flag?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the one and only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But there were the republican flags too, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were some flags that were not official flags. But the one that you mean, of course, needless to say, the thought wouldn't have occurred to anyone at all to set up any other flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Virijevic. I think this is a convenient time for our break because I'm about to move on to a different subject, a different area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will resume at just after a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Virijevic, let us continue, please. We talked about the day Vukovar fell, and you were telling us about what had been going on on that day. What you just told us about, which time of day was this, and what do you remember about that afternoon and evening, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: If memory serves, this was sometime in the afternoon. Might have been at about 2 or 3.00 in the afternoon that the whole thing drew to a close. I was very tired, extremely tired, and the first thing I wished for after it was all over was to take off somewhere, get a proper rest. That's one thing. And my other motive was to leave the area as soon as possible. It was all going smoothly. Nothing much was happening. I had been all along the front line. Thanks to my good luck, I was never seriously wounded aside from a number of minor injuries. Since now there was peace, but there were unexploded mines and ordinance all over the place, mines laid by the Croats. Some of our own mortar shells, unexploded, lying around. I just upped sticks with my unit, the squad, or what remained of the squad, those who were not wounded. I went to that cellar in Pavle's house where we set out from that very morning, and we crossed the road to Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that afternoon you went to Pavle's house and you rested; right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was fed up with war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there alone in that house. Aca Gvozdenovic was with me. I was his commander. Zeljko Sinikovic was there as well and another officer whose name escapes me. It was past 5.00. It was getting dark, but it's difficult to get my bearings exactly. Time of day didn't mean much because I had other things on my mind. Anyway, our commander came over. He said, "Get your equipment and get going; get a shift on." We said, "Where to?" He said, "You're off to Ovcara. It seems there's something going on there." My reaction was I kept silent, but I thought to myself silently how much longer. I was beginning to hope that it was all over, but a new order came and we got into the Puchs. It was a vehicle that our unit used. And we just drove straight to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember how many vehicles altogether you had?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It's been 15 years, especially in view of the nature of the things going on, but I think we had a total of three Puch vehicles. About three of those, but I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Virijevic, do you remember who was in the same vehicle as you? Who else?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Some men from my squad, those who were still fit enough to fight. Aca Gvozdenovic was the driver. Zeljko Sinikovic was with me, and -- let me see if I can remember. Let me see if I can remember who else was there. Two of them, and I can't remember the rest, except there was one soldier who was wounded, but I don't think he was there at the time, and there was a volunteer who was a member of the unit. He was in that Puch too. His name was Zoran Ivanovic. And believe it or not, I can't remember anybody else. I can't remember all of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about your commander? He was with you, right, or in a different vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was the end of the war and we were friends, but we complied with the subordination principle in a very strict way. He was at the head of the column, in the first Puch to leave. And Mladen Maric, who was company commander, had returned by this time. He was still in charge of the company because the other man was wounded. He wasn't up to date with what was going on. And I think he was in another vehicle, but I'm not sure. If memory serves me, I think he was in the first vehicle, and I myself was in the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When the commander arrived to get you, you and the other people who were staying in Pavle's house, do you remember who drove his vehicle, the vehicle that he was in?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The person driving his vehicle was warrant officer second class Stevo Bisic. He was a professional driver with our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us what you remember about when you arrived at Ovcara in your vehicles? Was that the first time you went to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first and last time that we went there in an organised manner. Once we arrived, we realised there was a hangar there and a group of people inside it. Stacks of hay next to it, that's one thing I remember, and a length of rope marking the point up to which we were allowed to go. They were just standing there. We left our vehicles. And what I was thinking about at the time was why we were there, because when we arrived everything was peaceful. I was look around to see if there was anything dodgy going on, but it was all peaceful and that was the first impression I had upon arriving. So there, that's what I remember. Let me say something else. The people there averaged about 30 years of age. I think -- and they looked cleaner and generally better than we did. They seemed quite fit, which is something I wasn't expecting, given the prolonged siege of Vukovar, the siege that we had maintained. They looked like a neat military unit, good, fit soldiers, clean-shaven.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll get to that, we'll get to the description of the people you found there, but let me ask you something about your previous observation. You say that because you were told that there was some problems, once there, you were looking left and right to see if anything was the matter and you failed to observe anything that set your mind thinking, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just want to place an objection on the record. Again, the summary of this witness' testimony with regard to this section, he will testify to his contacts with Prosecution Witness P-001. Again, we're involved in all sorts of facts well outside any of the disclosure or summary of facts provided to the Prosecution. This is now the second witness that I have objected to or we've objected to within two days of trial. At this point we're not asking that he be restricted from introducing any of this testimony and we're not asking to strike. However, we are asking that we receive additional facts into this -- into these contested areas before these witnesses take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. I would point out for all Defence teams that what the rule contemplates is that the summary will outline the facts about which the witness will testify. What Mr. Weiner points out about this witness is entirely well-founded. The summary does not give an indication in any way of the nature of the facts which are now being led from the witness. Therefore, the need to comply with the rule will have to be taken into more close consideration by each Defence team. Now, the rule doesn't require that you provide a full detailed statement covering every word the witness will speak about, but there must at least be an indication of the material facts about which the evidence of the witness will go. If that is not done, there are a number of potential consequences. The first of them is that you may be allowed to lead the evidence, but that it will be necessary to adjourn the cross-examination so that the witness would have to remain or go away and come back at another time. Another consequence is that you may not be allowed to lead certain evidence. I just use those two of illustrations of the possible consequences. Every circumstance could open up different ones. You need to be aware of those and be sure that the summaries provided are an adequate compliance with the requirements and spirit of the rule. Now, at the moment nothing is called for by Mr. Weiner, so we will take no specific action in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Virijevic, you started telling us about how you entered the hangar and saw those people. You gave us your judgement about their age. But you said that they were Croatian soldiers. Were they in uniforms or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: All of them were in civilian clothes. When I said "soldiers", I meant that their appearance was such that they would have made good soldiers. That's how they looked to me. They seemed fit. That's what I was trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to anyone or approach them? Did you get closer?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you stay longer? Did you stay for a while, in the hangar or not?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, I didn't even enter the hangar. I just came to the entrance but didn't go further, so it wasn't even close enough to the rope that separated them. There was no need for me. I had no business there in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see whether any of the people from your group talked to them?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was one member of our group, Aziz Memic. I stood some 5 to 6 metres behind him and he entered into a verbal duel with somebody from that group who came out of that group and introduced himself as Big Dzo. They started a conversation. I didn't hear what they were talking about. The conversation ended soon thereafter, and nothing of significance happened, nothing worth mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever find out who talked to Memic? Who was it who talked to him?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier I was curious. I have to tell you that, as a soldier, I was impressed by the attitude of this Croat. He acted honourably. He came out, he stepped out in front of his people. So I asked Borce who this person might be, and he said, Well, that was Filip Karaula. I learned that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who is Borce?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Borce Karanfilov was security commander in our unit, I mean the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, or rather, do you have any idea as to how many people there were?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I made two observations. The first one was that as soon as we came there, I was struck by the fact that the troops who were around there securing the perimeter were bearing very new, brand new uniforms, and we had been there with two months without any new equipment. So I was struck by that. And my second observation was, I didn't really count the people, but I think there might have been some 50 of them. That's my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "around 50," does this mean that there could have been less or more?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Not less, because the other part of the hangar was in the dark so one couldn't see everyone. So it definitely wasn't less than 50. It could have only been more than 50, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned this, you said that a part of the hangar was in the dark. Does it mean that the other part had light?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't know how come this was so, but I know that when I arrived, there was light shining in the area where these people were. I don't know how this was set up, but we could see people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just another question in relation to this. You were in the third vehicle. I assume that you were among the last to approach the area. Did you see what others did? Did they enter inside? Were there any problems or conversations before they entered the hangar?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: From what I could see from the third vehicle, when Bisic Stevo stopped the car, I saw him discussing something with a man wearing the JNA uniform. It was a heated discussion and he sort of pushed him lightly away. But I didn't see or hear what it was. When I approached later, I heard that this was some man called Petar, a commander. And I don't know what it was all about, but later on he told us that an order had been issued from above, saying that these people must not be touched. That's what I heard from this captain whom I didn't know and who wasn't from my unit. I had no previous contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Transcript line 39 -- page 39, line 3, it says "Petar, a commander." I don't think that you mentioned a name. You said something else.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I said "captain", I said "captain" and not "Petar". I was referring to the rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this bit where you were told that there was an order coming from above, what did they mean by "above"?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: They meant Belgrade, from Belgrade. That's what "above" meant. And we knew who was in Belgrade, chief of general staff, and so on. So we didn't really ask for further details. We didn't ask for any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time hear anything about this alleged problem, if there ever was any?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked my commander. We were friends privately, but at work it was strictly business. So I asked him, "Why did we come? What was the reason?" And he said, "Some drunk captain came and started threatening the prisoners." That's the explanation he gave me, saying that that was the reason we had to go there that night. My comment was, Hey, classmate, that's how we used to refer to each other when we were alone, I said, "Did we really need to send out an anti-terrorist platoon to straighten out some drunk captain?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How long did you stay there, in your view.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not very good with figures, as I told you, but I think it was about half an hour. Ten minutes, more or less. We didn't see much, but everything that we saw was absolutely calm. So we got back into our vehicles and went back to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say that everything was calm. Let me ask you this directly: As you were leaving, did you hear any shooting in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Since I am an experienced marksman and I am the army champion in that category, I'm quite qualified, but there was absolutely nothing. There was some shooting in Vukovar but not in that area. There was nothing going on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, just a few words about your relations with your commander. You said that you were classmates, and you mentioned several times how you were on very good times privately. Is that how it remained after Vukovar? Did you continue seeing him, socialising with him, not only while on duty but also privately?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you've known somebody since 1983, if you met somebody when you were 15-year-olds, if you were friends throughout and even trained judo and were together in the same sports club, it is natural that we remained friends all the way up until he left. I don't know where he went. We were family friends, so it wasn't just a friendship between us. Our children were friends, as was natural between two friends. It was a normal, friendly communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Following his departure, as you say, did he ever get in touch with you by phone, in writing, or in any other way?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. And it hurts me. I see no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you think that there was a reason?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not on my part. No. We were friends for a great many years. It's not clear not only to me -- rather, not only did he get in touch with me, he didn't get in touch with anyone in Belgrade, and I was wondering why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Virijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed by examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have a couple of questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If the witness is ready, my first question is: Would you explain to the Court your axis of action in September of '91 -- rather, in November of '91?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact name of the street. I don't want to get it wrong. I think it was Augusta Cesarca Street. It was a green zone that was across from Pavle's house. So we were on the right flank of the unit commanded by Captain Bojkovski Sasa at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was on your right side?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately a lot of commanders died and I can't remember exactly who was there in November. But that was the unit under the command of Adem Bajic, an infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you get to know Sasa Bojkovski well at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We worked in the barracks. I knew him prior to that. Yes, yes, I got to know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: During the war in Vukovar, was the person called (redacted) ever wounded?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not even a scratch. That person was the commander. He was naturally in the rear. So, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Can we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have Exhibit 171 brought up on our screens, or rather my assistant will play that for us. But before that appears on our monitors, I would like to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a film called "The 100 Days of Vukovar"?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I've seen parts of it but not the entire film. I find that a bit saddening so I try to avoid these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you are familiar of its existence and you've seen parts of it; right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that shown now, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this film?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this particular bit. Not the whole thing, but this was shown on our T.V. several times, this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What does the very beginning say?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: "The 100 days of Vukovar".

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please not cover your mouth with your hand because I'm having trouble hearing you. Thank you. Do you recognise the person in this frame whose voice we have just heard?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This is Bojkovski, whose last name now appears to be Bojkovic, Sasa. He was a member of my unit, my commander's unit. We exchanged positions. We assumed their positions at one point and they moved elsewhere. I know the man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You saw this film in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, part of it, not the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this film was shown throughout Croatia, or just in some parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you watched parts of this film and when you heard Sasa Bojkovski say what he does, which other name was dropped as the person who was allegedly uttering these words in this film?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I even said it once. I once met Bojkovski. Somebody quoted Radic as saying this, because that's what the film itself suggests, which is plain wrong. This excerpt has been run and rerun and it always said Radic. I was greatly amazed that there was nobody to do anything about it, and deny it, because there's not even the vaguest physical resemblance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just to make things clear for the Trial Chamber, why do they say Radic, and which Radic do they have in mind? What exactly did you hear when you heard parts of this movie?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You're asking this witness why someone else or why the people from Croatia who made the movie said it was Radic? That's for the producers, the director, the people who made the movie, not for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. The question to the witness is:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When he was listening to parts of this movie, as shown on Serbian T.V., was there a running commentary within the film itself as to who was saying those words, identifying the person uttering these words?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These words were attributed to the criminal Radic. That was the Croatian subtitles but that was deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they say which Radic they had in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Radic who was convicted -- rather, I apologise, indicted before the Hague Tribunal, to prove that he was a criminal. That was the nature of comment, the running commentary. I can't remember every single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was that the sound belonging to the film that you were watching?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These very words. I even asked Bojkovski, "What was that all about" and he said “Let it be, nobody’s bothering me.”

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll need to raise my working temperature, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have two very brief questions for you. Mr. Virijevic, I am Novak Lukic, counsel for Veselin Sljivancanin. I'll ask you two very short questions stemming from answers you provided to Mr. Domazet. You talked about the ethnic makeup of your own platoon, and you specified its ethnic makeup. Does the name of Saban Sabani ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me try to jog your memory. This is an ethnic Albanian who was for a while a member of -- well, for my client you know. But if you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: You probably mean Idriz Sabani, not Saban Sabani.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your information is better than mine.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: He comes from the same place as I and we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. He was a member of the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. My next question stems from your answer when Mr. Domazet asked you about the flag that was eventually hoisted up on the water tower. You were surprised by the very nature of that question, so let me ask you this: Do you know about my client's feelings about the Yugoslav flag and about Yugoslavdom as such?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I know him well enough to be able to say that. I think he was even going too far. We even made jokes at his expense, because he was so extremely pro-Yugoslav. "I kiss the very grave of our Partizan struggle," that sort of thing, along these lines. It was exaggerated -- well, not really exaggerated. You know what I mean. But he was certainly emphatically pro-Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know this thing about kissing the grave. The Trial Chamber doesn't. I'm not going into those details. How did he feel about the Chetniks and their insignia, insignia that were being supported in Vukovar? That much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about what happened in Vukovar itself, but I can tell you in very general terms, whoever wanted to be expelled from his unit, all they needed to do was just mention the very hint of it and then they would be out in no time all, before they could brink an eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. These are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Weiner, is it more practical to proceed immediately or to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Either. A small break now would be fine, whatever the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have to have a half hour break because of the redaction. You would have 10 or 12 minutes before we head to break. I think a break now might be more practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn until just after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I spotted the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not a high level of similarity, actually. Your Honour, may I deal with two small matters. It's quite simply this: The Prosecution called three principal witnesses in relation to the 18th of November. They were not protected witnesses; they are clearly Vezmarovic, Vojnovic and Vasiljevic -- Vukosavljevic. At no time was it ever put by the Defence counsel that the anti-terrorist unit came on that day, had dealings with those officers or those units; that there was any conversation with Filip Karaula. There was nothing said at all. So as the situation now stands, the Defence are intending, and clearly are calling witnesses, as to this topic, where our witnesses have had no opportunity of either accepting or denying that that actually occurred. And it puts the Prosecution at a significant disadvantage. And it's not a case that the Defence are caught unaware, because Witness 001 was on the 65 ter list and clearly indicated what his evidence was going to be. That is one submission that we are concerned about. At this time we don't know exactly whether we'll make an application to recall, but I merely air it at this time. The second matter: I would ask the Court's indulgence in allowing me to cross-examine this witness on certain areas, and I'll explain quite simply why. The Court is well aware that two members of the Prosecution team have gone on to greater fields. Mr. Weiner has come in very late and he did not deal with this area of evidence specifically. He has read the case, but it's not the same as being actively involved in the case at that time. I dealt with these witnesses and I dealt with this topic, and I would ask the Court's indulgence to cross-examine this witness in relation to these matters, and Mr. Weiner then to continue on other topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're seeking, really, to split the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. And it will be an application that we will be making on some other witnesses because clearly the way things have developed within the Prosecution team, and it's no one's fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does any Defence counsel wish to deal with the first of those issues, which is essentially a failure to raise this aspect of the Defence case in the course of cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses? Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to remind everyone in this courtroom that this subject was tackled by a protected witness of the OTP, the very protected witness that was mentioned here today. I personally cross-examined that witness and confronted him with this position regarding the date of his departure, right here in this courtroom, when he left for that particular place. He said in cross-examination that it was possible the date was the one mentioned by the Defence witnesses.
