I have to say this protected witness came to testify after the witness brought up by my learned friend, Witness Vojnovic, Witness Vezmarovic and Witness Vukosavljevic, these three witnesses. The Defence had no reason to ask these witnesses anything about this fact simply because they didn't speak to the fact while being examined by my learned friend. The only witness to speak about the arrival and the date was the protected witness that I cross-examined on that, making it clear to him that there had been witnesses suggesting a date very different from the one that he insisted on. It was this very witness who agreed with me that my position was possible. For this reason I did not believe that the Defence was under any obligation to question Vezmarovic, Vukosavljevic, and Vojnovic on something that hadn't been raised in the examination-in-chief or the original statements. I think we took the right course of action, and we only examined on these matters the witnesses who spoke directly to these facts. As for the other motion of my learned friend, it is my belief that we should try to make everyone's work easier to the extent possible. But the rule that we have always applied was one counsel, one witness. And I think the OTP enjoys a much more convenient position than the Defence teams in terms of our resources and our ability to prepare our respective cases. The Defence teams have not been able to avail themselves of this possibility when cross-examining witnesses. It is in the name of equality of arms that I think we should keep the same principle now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the first matter, the legal interests of Mr. Radic's defence is, in no way challenged. As for the other issue, in principle I shall oppose that. However, out of professional respect I choose not to oppose this motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to add something to what my colleague, Mr. Vasic, has said in relation to the first subject. If I'm wrong, may Mr. Moore please correct me. I've been slightly taken aback. As far as I remember, the testimony of Witness P001 about his arrival at Ovcara was submitted to us through an addendum received immediately before he entered the courtroom. In his statement that we had received from the OTP at the disclosure stage, there was no mention whatsoever of the fact that he had gone to Ovcara at all. I think that's the way things are. If I'm wrong, I think Mr. Moore will correct me. But I think the very subject of his addendum was about Ovcara, and I did cross-examine the witness about that. That's the first thing. Secondly, speaking of this issue, namely, whether members of the anti-terrorist company arrived at Ovcara on the 18th or not, if that was of substantial interest to Mr. Moore and the Prosecutor, and if they had known about this, they should have asked their own witnesses about this and they should have laid a path open to us, knowing what their own witnesses knew about this. But I really can't be expected to raise issues that I don't know about. I may end up speculating, but my inferences at this stage, the OTP don't want to know. I might as well be wrong; please correct me if I am. As for this other issue, I know that I was once denied an objection when my colleague Mr. Bulatovic was cross-examining a witness. I am really fully familiar with this particular difficulty, what the OTP have just raised. I've been thinking along the following lines: I might have a motion to raise when my own case starts due to the scope of some of the subjects that need covering. I think we shall be in a position where both counsel will have to take part with certain witnesses, and I certainly hope that a relevant decision will be made when the time arises. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Firstly, our witnesses at no time spoke about the anti-terrorist unit coming on the 18th, so we had no reason to know that there was a suggestion of the anti-terrorist unit coming on the 18th. So it's not a topic we would have dealt with in chief; we had no way of knowing about it. With respect to the addendum, that is being checked. In any event, if my learned friend were going to and know what their case is going to be, namely, that 001 did attend at Ovcara, they should -- and that was on the 18th, it should have been put to the three officers who were present at Ovcara on the 18th, dealing with the Mitnica battalion. As I say, we will check what the witness statement says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that going to be a lengthy process?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it's not as quick a process as it should be, I'm afraid. We try and go through the electronics. But from my own memory, there was reference by 001 - that was the reason he was called - was that he had been summoned to Ovcara and then basically returned. And that, from my memory, was included in his witness statement. By I, like Mr. Lukic, am trying to go back in time very quickly. But if Your Honour gives me a moment, I can check the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make a suggestion which will mean that we don't waste any time? Could I seek, perhaps, a Court ruling in relation to whether it will be permissible to cross-examine, and the other matter, whether the matters should be put or not, can be clarified once the statements have been looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've just been casting my eye down your document, the 65 ter statement for the witness, 001, dated the 29th of August, 2005, and it includes no reference to that date at all, if that's of help, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I seem to remember that there was reference to him being called and then having to return. But, as I say, that can be checked. There's no doubt at all there was an addendum, but there was reference to him being called to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of the need to clarify recollection, we will not make any observation about the first matter at this present time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As to the second motion, Mr. Moore, the Chamber is of the view that there is not a sufficient justification for departure from the normal practice of one witness, one counsel. Obviously had this happened, as it were, as a matter of unexpected emergency this morning or last night, our position would probably have been different. But there has been time to consider and prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I take it, then, that that will apply to the application that my learned friend will make on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you can not take that. We have no application from Mr. Sljivancanin. There was a musing of a possibility. If an application is made, we will have to consider the application on its merits. Its merits will have to be very distinctive in order to overcome what we have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're thrust into stardom, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no visible witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we go into private session just for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've testified that you've known number 1 for many years.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you said that you first met him in 1983. Did you mean 1973?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1973. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you served together?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We attended the secondary military school in Sarajevo together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You served in the military together.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the mandatory military service, that's one thing, whereas the schooling at school is a different matter. Yes, we were together in the secondary school. And when you attend the military school, then you don't have to serve the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A different use of terms -- terminology that we use in the States. You were both together in the same unit? Yes?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from 1973, when we were in the same classroom. We were schooled together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was a good friend?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you played sports together?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he treated you fairly, and you the same to him?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as friends normally treat each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And you trusted him?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, without limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you asked him that -- you asked him, "Why were we called out?" because you knew that he would tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At least I believed that he would tell me the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's because you trusted his word.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's because -- and you trusted his word because he was honest with you.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add to that: Not only with me. As a commander, he was sincere in his dealings with all members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you know him as a sincere and honest person.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the period while we were still friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And a person who you can rely upon what he says.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the time while we were still socialising.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to a few other issues in relation to your unit. Your unit returned back to Belgrade in November 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you remained part of the Guards Motorised Brigade until what year?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until retirement in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go back to November 21st, 1991, through the end of the year. Were you or any members of your unit ever interviewed or questioned in relation to the member -- to the murder of prisoners at Ovcara? From November 21st, 1991, through the end of the year, were you or members of your unit ever interviewed or questioned in relation to the murder of prisoners at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What's more, I didn't know that anything had happened at Ovcara. In my view, nothing happened there. So for that reason, nobody ever questioned me about anything, nor did I see a reason for anyone to question me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. What about 1992? Were you or members of your unit questioned about the murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can now speak only on my behalf. Nobody ever asked me anything about murders at Ovcara, nor did I know that anything had happened in Ovcara. I'm now referring to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about members of the Guards Brigade? Had you heard of anyone being questioned about the murders at Ovcara in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that either way. Since I am a non-commissioned officer, not everything was available to me. I didn't know about everything. Perhaps yes; perhaps no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's return to your unit. Were you or any members of your unit, in 1991 or 1992, asked to provide a written report or a statement in relation to the persons who were murdered at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know -- actually, I didn't even know that any murders had taken place. Nobody asked for a written statement or report, nor did we provide any. I have to qualify this, once again, by saying that I am speaking only on my own behalf. On the 1st of June, 2002, I moved into another unit as a result of which I lost touch with a lot of people who had served with me previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then were you aware, in 1991 or 1992, of any investigation in relation to the murder of prisoners at Ovcara? Were you aware in 1991 or 1992 of any investigation being under way?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally didn't know anything. Once again, I am only speaking from my own angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you, having been a police officer or a military police officer previously, you're aware that when a serious crime occurs, police must act quickly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me clarify: I was a military policeman in the squad for anti-sabotage activity aimed at locating mines and explosives. There is another squad in charge of what you referred about that deals with criminal forensics. I'm not sure about their exact name, but they deal with such issues. And I was not informed about their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I know that, sir. What I'm just asking you is, based on your police training, you're aware that if a serious crime occurs, the police must act quickly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You have to secure the scene; you have to collect evidence, locate witnesses. Aren't those required?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You described it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You have to interview witnesses, interview suspects.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And all of these tasks are in the gamut of this special squad that I told you about, and we don't interfere in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there was a special squad within the Guards Motorised Brigade that completed these assignments or were responsible for these assignments.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With the battalion of the military police, within the Guards Brigade, within it I think there was what we called crime suppression squad. I think that each brigade has it, and ours definitely had it. And this squad performs the work that you described - securing the crime scene, locating witnesses, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they also have to do certain forensic types of work - find evidence, secure evidence, collect evidence.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's their job. They have no other job but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And like yourself, you received anti-terrorist training, they received training in this area of evidence collection and forensic analysis.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very technical training. In addition to the military police training, they receive additional training for crime technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to your unit as the so-called cream of the crop, the best of the best. These police officers, the officers in this unit, in this crime suppression and investigation unit, were they also the best within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was of too low a rank to be able to give you my judgement. I think that they were well trained for the job that they were performing. But, once again, who am I to say so? I am not competent enough to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just one more question in a related area, sir. In 1991 and in 1992, were you aware of anyone being disciplined or punished for the murders that were committed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware, and I am now speaking in the capacity of an ordinary citizen. No, I am not aware of that. You know that there was a distribution of assignments and tasks within the army, which means that we didn't know what somebody else was doing. So it may have been done by somebody else; it's just that I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, if someone was arrested or someone was punished for a massacre, it's something that you would have heard about; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely I would have heard, yes, because it was a unit where all of us served. We were all housed in the same place, so it would be hard to conceal that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never heard anything in 1991 and 1992 of anyone being punished, as you all were in that same barracks?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear. But, once again, I am emphasising that my job was such that I didn't have a duty to try to learn of such things. Even though it was a small unit, not all of us knew what the other person was doing. Everybody did their job, as is typical in any army, and everybody was responsible for their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, again, sir, if someone was arrested for hundreds of murders, you would have heard about that. If someone from your unit or someone from your Guards Motorised Brigade was arrested, you would have known about that.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have definitely heard about it, and I believe that had somebody done that, a member of the Guards Brigade, he would have been arrested back in Vukovar- I firmly believe in this- because that was the state of affairs within the unit. We were brought to task for minor things, let alone for something of that scale. I am now referring to minor disciplinary infringements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you also know that no one was punished in Vukovar for any of those murders. From November 21st to the end of the year, no one was punished in Vukovar for any of those murders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you in relation to the entire Vukovar. Could you please be more specific? You mean my unit? Because Vukovar is quite a broad term. There were many units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of anyone being punished - just yes or no - were you aware of anyone being punished in Vukovar, from November 21st to the end of the year, for the murders that occurred in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember -- it's not that I remember. It's just that I don't know. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to take you back to November 18th, 19th and 20th. Do you recall being advised of any orders where soldiers were warned that the Geneva Conventions must be observed? On those three days, do you recall being advised by your supervisor or being advised by Commander Mrksic down that the Geneva Conventions must be observed? And that's with regard to prisoners.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're referring to my unit; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for something like that, because in our training we received instruction as to what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you a very specific question. Were you advised by order --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the witness needs to complete his answer. He didn't complete it, and perhaps it would be clear what the response is. He was cut off before he was allowed to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the essence of his response had become clear, and Mr. Weiner was bringing him back to the particular question. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Did you receive an order, from the Commander Mrksic down to your level, on the 18th, 19th or 20th of November, warning soldiers that the Geneva Conventions must be observed with regard to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You interrupted me as I was about to answer. Every soldier received this in writing before we were deployed to Vukovar, and I think there was no need to repeat it every 20 days or so. All of us received it in writing, the explanation on what war is and how we need to conduct ourselves. We received it on the second day after our arrival in Negoslavci, all of us, to the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: On the 18th, 19th and 20th of November, on those three dates, did you receive that order and warning from Commander Mrksic that was sent down to your unit? I'm looking for those days.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in those three days, we received no additional instructions or orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive an order during those days that disobedience or unsoldierly behaviour must be prevented? On those three days.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to answer. This goes without saying. We didn't receive it in the form of a specific order. But we were professional soldiers. There was no need to issue orders every day about something that was self-understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive an order that commanders at all levels will be responsible for their areas, and no one has the right of retribution or revenge? Did you receive that order and warning on the 18th, 19th or 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking on my own behalf. No more than that. I did not see such an order. But, again, I must say, this was understood. There was no need to have such an order issued. We were trained professional soldiers, after all. As for any other units, whether they received anything or not, I really can't tell you. I'm in no position to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you also made aware as -- were you also made aware on those three days that acts of retribution and revenge had been committed by TO members, and as a result they were warning all soldiers not to take those acts and commands to ensure that such acts were not taken? Do you recall that being provided on the 18th, 19th or 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, speaking for myself, I did not hear of anyone committing any murders in Vukovar at the time. I wasn't moving about Vukovar that much. I was just trying to survive, get home to my family safe and in one piece, if possible. I did not receive any order or instruction as to what I was supposed to be doing or preventing, simply because I did not know there was anything going on at the time that needed preventing, to begin it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, did you receive notice on the 18th, 19th and 20th of November that persons who take revenge or retribution, or actually soldiers who take revenge or retribution must be arrested? Did you receive that order?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received no such order. There was no need. We weren't near any detainees at the time. I'm talking about right after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, were you aware that General Zivota Panic issued those orders that I just mentioned to you? Were you aware of that, sir? All those orders we've been discussing in the last five minutes, were you aware that General Zivoda Panic issued those orders to subordinate troops? Were you aware of that on the 18th, 19th or 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's too high a level for me to know anything about. Zivota Panic was chief of the general staff, or his deputy, as far as I remember. It's a possibility, but I certainly have no direct and personal knowledge of that. I was just a warrant officer second class, after all, and a general is always a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have some other questions for you about Vukovar. While in Vukovar, sir, you saw soldiers from other units and detachments; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct in part. I did see some, but the combat deployment was such that they were moving left and right all the time and we didn't cross that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at times you saw some members of the Vukovar TO?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically along my own axis, I never saw a single one - I repeat - TO members. I had two volunteers in my own unit, two volunteers from Vukovar who were with me throughout. They felt as members of our unit, and they did some logistics for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you had volunteers working with you. Did you see any of the so-called Chetniks while you were there in Vukovar, before or after the so-called liberation?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's start with before. The composition and rank of our unit implied that we would have been highly irritated by the presence of any Chetniks, and I'm sure they would have been irritated by us, perhaps even more so. The answer is I didn't see any. I just didn't. It was incompatible with our interpretation of war and struggle. We still all wore the five-pointed star on our caps, but we just didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after the so-called liberation, did you see any along the streets?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the liberation, well, when I reached the cellar - I only spent a brief time out in the street - I saw all sorts of things. There were all sorts of people moving about. People in uniform, unkempt people. There were some dressed in uniforms that weren't our military uniforms but rather some other uniforms. They didn't look like soldiers, their physical appearance I mean. I'm talking about the time I spent walking along that road before I reached the cellar. But in that area, right then and there, you certainly couldn't see anyone mistreating or unsettling, disturbing, anybody else. That might have been just out of respect to our own unit, but I can't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see Arkan or any of his men on the 18th, 19th or 20th, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You say "God forbid," sir. Had you ever worked with any of those groups previously, the Chetniks, Arkan and his men, or a number of those volunteer groups prior to that -- prior to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never, nothing. Never did we do anything with them or would have done. If we had been asked to, we probably would have stood up to that order at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Because you realise that there's a difference in levels of training between the training that you had and the training that these other groups have, these quasi-military, if you want to call them, volunteer groups.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were probably people doing their regular military term, and that was all the military training they had. Unlike them, we had undergone training that was a lot longer and more complex in comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And these groups were not as disciplined as your unit; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely correct. Not just those groups. No other unit was as disciplined as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that some of these groups of volunteers, whether they're Chetniks or Arkan's people, were drinking and looting? Had you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I locked myself up in that cellar. I didn't see anything; I didn't hear anything like that. As far as I know, if Arkan ever was in Vukovar, he must have come from somewhere else, from a totally different direction. Not during the siege, not after the fall, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you lock yourself up in that cellar?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not lock myself up. I came to that cellar on the 18th. We went to Ovcara and I again returned to that cellar. I didn't literally lock myself up. I was just spending most of my time in the cellar or just outside. It's not a cellar, really. It's like a room underneath a house used for private business by a man who built the house. So when I say "cellar", that's what I mean. What I meant to say is I spent most of my time there. I was amongst the most senior people in that group, the oldest people. I was fed up with everything. And after the 18th, my only objective was to survive, to save my hide and not get maimed or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you knew these other groups, the ones you referred to which you wouldn't work with, some of these other groups of volunteers, you knew that they were prone to violence, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't anywhere near me, but my assumption is they could not have had the same level of discipline that we had. But anything is possible. There was certainly nothing like that happening near where I was. I did not witness any of these volunteer groups committing acts of violence. But it's the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- I'm asking you, sir. Listen to my question, please. Were you aware that these groups were prone to violence? Not that you saw it directly. Based on what you had heard, because you said "God forbid" you would ever work with these groups. Were you aware that they were prone to violence?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some sort, yes. There wasn't a group like us. We just refused to identify with someone who was not as well trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And being some sort of prone to violence - that's your statement - you knew that these groups could cause a very serious danger.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Vukovar, did you see any orders coming down from Colonel Mrksic or filtering down to your level that the volunteers must be trained according to the rules of the Geneva Convention? Did you see any such order?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was just a lowly soldier. If there was an order like that, the commander would have seen it, not me. It wasn't necessary to pass it down, all the way down the chain, to me. I was a squad commander. I didn't see an order like that myself. I'm not saying it was never issued, I'm just saying I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the volunteers, the Chetniks, TO members, being trained according to the Geneva Conventions while in Vukovar? Had you heard of such training occurring?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question. I simply don't know. I was a front line soldier. I was just looking to save my life. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you, on the other hand, were a member of an elite unit in the Guards Motorised Brigade, the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it was a section of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The unit was comprised of officers, sergeants and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit, my platoon, comprised officers and NCOs, but when you say sergeants, I suppose that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: NCOs, yes.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about my platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the other platoons?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other platoons comprised a commander and komandiri, lower level commanders. The rest were others doing their regular military term, conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you received special training to be in that anti-terrorist unit; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't just training every day; it was training all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were trained to deal with terrorists.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we were set up for originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were trained to deal with rebel groups.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Groups of terrorists as opposed to a single terrorist. Groups.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the middle of training when the war broke out. Terrorism, do you know what that means? One, two, three minor groups. But there was a war on suddenly and we were in the middle of something that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were trained to deal in hostage situations.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were trained for rapid intervention.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever ordered, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Being a highly trained and specialised unit, your unit could have been used to protect prisoners in a hostile or difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anyone had ordered us to, then yes. But this was the end of the war. We were decimated by this time. Many had been wounded. Many were at the military academy hospital in Belgrade. But yes, in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your unit could be utilised to free hostages or prisoners being held as hostages.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were trained for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your unit could be used to prevent an attack on a government building or a prison facility.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on November 20th, 1991, your unit was not ordered to guard the prisoners at Ovcara on a 24-hour -- over a 24-hour basis; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On November --

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it had received that order, it certainly would have carried out that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It would have carried out the order. Your unit wasn't ordered to continue to take necessary action to protect the prisoners at Ovcara from harm on November 20th. Were you ordered to do that?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I found out about the prisoners after the 18th. But there were no orders. I personally at least, from where I stand now, we personally didn't know on the 20th that there were prisoners in the hangar there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were not ordered on the 20th to remove any TO members, Chetniks or volunteers, from the area of the detention facility at Ovcara. You didn't receive those order on the 20th either.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 20th we received no combat orders at all, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, were you aware of any orders being issued that TO members, Chetniks or volunteers were not to be in the area of the Ovcara detention facility? Were you aware of any orders of that kind on November 20th?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there were orders that were issued, but at my level they certainly didn't reach me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is: Were you aware of any such order?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "were".

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of any order that the TO members, the Chetniks, the volunteers, were not allowed in the area of the detention facility at Ovcara? Were you aware of any order of that kind being issued? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no knowledge of that at all. It wasn't my job to know. I personally knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have no records, any written records, as to what you did in November of 1990, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No records.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You have no diary of what you did in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. I didn't keep a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1991. I said 1990. 1991, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine. Same answer: I didn't keep a diary. But we had people in charge of that in our unit. And I didn't really have time for anything like that. I was just looking to save my life. I wasn't thinking about logbooks or diaries or anything. It was a full-scale front line war, shooting every day, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you have no agenda or calendar indicating what you did on each day of November 1990.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not sure if the -- if my commander, 001, kept an agenda or anything. But I certainly knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. The commander, it's not a mistake, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you -- when we talk about 1991, you're not aware, actually, what day of the week November 18th was, are you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The 19th?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Or the 20th?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no idea what day it was the 1st of September, especially contemporaneously. It's not something that I keep in mind. I don't have a good head for figures, and I don't even try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 19th and 20th, you were mostly at that house, either in the basement, if you want to call it the cellar, the basement, or in the house.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the house. The house was ruined. I slept underground, and I would spend some time in the front yard of that house. It was peaceful. There wasn't much going on. But it's been too long. It's difficult to think back and remember everything, all the nitty-gritty. I can just tell you where I spent most of my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you weren't walking around in downtown Vukovar during those dates, the 18th, 19th and 20th.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, walking around?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just strolling around. On the 19th and 20th, things were more relaxed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I think it was on the 20th that I took a 15-minute drive to the center of Vukovar, downtown Vukovar as you say, in a Puch, just to see what it's like, the center. But that's as much time as I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on the 19th and 20th, there were civilians walking around. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was driving through, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were various soldiers walking around.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers, yes, there were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were --

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been a war. It's the way things usually are after a war has just ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were press people walking around --

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. There were journalists around but not with me, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were photographers walking around.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around Vukovar, you mean, the 19th, 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were television people walking around. Television and radio people.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people were celebrating.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't until much later on T.V. that I realised there had been celebrations. Not while there, on the spot. I hadn't really realised. I saw the first footage of these celebrations in downtown Vukovar several days later when I came home. I don't know how much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it was a relaxed atmosphere, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You might say it was relaxed, as far as that term would have been appropriate at the time, after all that had happened. There had been combat operations going on for a long time, and now the atmosphere was more relaxed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people were wearing different parts of uniforms. People were wearing hats that didn't belong to the uniforms. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I saw much more on television later on than in those 15 minutes that I spent driving through the center. I saw more of it in the footage that I saw later on. Yes, there were people going on wearing all sorts of caps. They were just put on, that sort of thing. Yes, it's been known to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And a lot of the soldiers, including yourself, were not clean-shaven.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was such a dramatic lack of hygiene that if we had been clean-shaven, I think we would have ended up in a dermatology ward. I did have an electric shaver, so sometimes I would just trim my beard a little, just to not let myself slide altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You don't recall anything significant happening that afternoon, or the morning/afternoon of the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember nothing significant happening, nothing that would have drawn my attention. I certainly -- that would have attracted my attention. I remember nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you don't have -- recall anything significant happening to you on the morning or the afternoon of the 20th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th, nothing that meant anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were mainly back at that house where you had been staying or sleeping on the 19th and 20th.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent most of the time in the house or outside the house. I can't rule out the possibility that I drove over to Negoslavci on one occasion, perhaps, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you can't say what every member of your unit was doing on the 19th and 20th, can you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't say. I can talk about most in my squad, in my group, but I can't say all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, obviously, you have no records, you've maintained no records, now 15 years later, of what everybody was doing on the 19th and 20th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no notes or records. I had no wish to note anything down. I just wanted to erase all of those events and have no memory of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And some of the members of your unit were at various locations: Some were at the school; some were in other houses; some were walking around. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out the possibility. As I said, not everyone was next to me or where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you can't say where everyone was, where all members of your unit were, on the evening of November 19th, can you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 19th, no, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you can't say where you were on the evening -- where the members -- every member of your unit was, on the evening of the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been 15 years. I can't remember everything. There was nothing remarkable that I saw happening that would remain etched in my mind. I can't say that nothing happened anywhere, but nothing that I would notice or remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Basically, without any records or notes, there's nothing you can really recall 15 years later, you yourself can recall; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember important things. As for the dates, I'm not always fully certain about them. But in general, when it comes to important events, such as the fall of Vukovar, those things I remember. I remember the relief I felt on that day, because I thought that something positive had happened. This is precisely why I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said that, "as for the dates, I'm not always fully certain about them." You said previously that you're not good with dates or figures; isn't that correct? Or numbers.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You know facts but you really can't apply them to a particular date; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get back to this, but I want to ask you a few questions concerning a few other matters that were raised today. You were shown a video by learned counsel Borovic. Do you recall that? You were shown a video with a sergeant, I think, with a thick, thick moustache. A picture on a video.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a captain. One could see it on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And there was a mistake made as to the identity of that person by the speaker. You recall that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said that there wasn't even a vague resemblance of that person to Captain Radic. That was the phrase you used, "not even a vague resemblance" to Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's too late now, and this is something that the witness didn't state earlier. He didn't state this earlier that he bore no resemblance to Radic whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The phrase I have is "not even a vague resemblance." I can get it in the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have such a note, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 45, the phrase is "because there's not even the vaguest physical resemblance," is the phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't participate in the making of this film or documentary; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I watched it on television in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware that it was made by Croatians; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or, rather, I wasn't aware, but Mr. Borovic reminded me and then -- I simply paid no attention to who produced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you realise it was made by a person who did not know these soldiers or officers.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were able to make such a comparison, then it means it's either a case of bad intentions or lack of knowledge. No other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Because, if you know a person or you've known a person for a long time, you wouldn't make that type of mistake; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a big mistake? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if you've known Captain Radic for a number of years, not being a close friend, but if you've known him for a number of years, you're not going to make that mistake, mixing him up with someone else that doesn't even look like him. Isn't that correct? It's common sense.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if I was malevolent and wanted to set him up with something. But otherwise no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you have no evidence of any malevolence in that case, in this particular situation in this video.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no evidence. If it was the Croatians who produced it, I know that they were quite well informed about what was going on. That's my experience. They even published lists as to who held which position. So it's surprising that they would make such a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But - I apologise - I don't rule out the possibility that it was a case of lack of familiarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, it's obvious that you didn't participate in the evacuations which occurred between the 18th and the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even -- not even close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were not at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You don't know who was at the hospital, which members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, except for what I saw later on television, B92 and so on. But I don't have firsthand information, because our positions were quite distant from the hospital, in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So having seen this on the television, you know that there were press people at the hospital; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I saw this on television, and then later on I acquired some information about what was going on at the hospital when talking to our Sergeant Jovic, who had been wounded and was hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what conversations people from the press had with Captain Radic at the hospital, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know a single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You don't know what conversations members of the press had with Major Sljivancanin at the hospital, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the footage that was filmed earlier, when he was talking to a member of peacekeeping forces at the bridge. I think it was before the fall of Vukovar. That's all I know. I don't know anything else. And that kind of information wasn't really available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, again, you're not certain of the dates, isn't that correct, of that incident?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which incident? Which one do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The filming, you said, of Major Sljivancanin speaking to the peacekeeper. You said you thought that was prior to the so-called fall of Vukovar -- or the fall of Vukovar. You're not certain of any date on that, are you?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not certain, so I can't make any claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for timing, are we going to the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Until about 20 minutes to, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to put as few questions as possible in my redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's deal with the last topic. You said out of all that footage, you remember one in particular involving the peacekeeper, and you spoke about that. When did you watch that?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched that footage when I came home, after all the combat had ended, and that's how I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that why you can't be certain about the date of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. How could I remember something like that? This was transpiring in a place distant from our positions, and I'm trying not to memorise things that are of no concern of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My learned friend put many questions to you as to what you were able to observe or what you were able to know about the tasks of other units, and he especially focused on Territorial Defence and the Chetniks. Were you in the position to see or to exercise any control over the conduct of those units in combat?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody in their right mind would send Chetniks anywhere near us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mentioned Arkan, you said, "God forbid," and as far as I remember, that referred to him and his people, not to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you at that point have in mind some other units, volunteer or Chetniks units, or did you only have Arkan in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular point I only had Arkan in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When asked whether these other units had a lesser degree of discipline, you said yes, but I don't think that it was clear enough. I think that you continued on, saying that you believed your unit was the most disciplined one. Do you mean more than other JNA units?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was the most disciplined unit which exercised a great degree of self-discipline, too. When I say "self-discipline," that means that each of us was well aware of our own duties and responsibilities. We required no additional instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that in line with the explanation you gave as to how you received the rules of conduct once and there was no need for you to receive it again?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went through four or five years of very serious military training, so naturally there was no need for us to repeat to us on a daily basis something that we had known already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since my colleague asked you about the other units, do you know whether other units received such instructions or not?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, when you are on the front, you have no time to inquire as to who got which instructions. You're just trying to save your life. So I was in no position to inquire about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One of the questions was whether you saw anybody committing any crime. You said no. And my question to you is: Had you encountered a situation where somebody was taking revenge on somebody, would you have prevented that? Would you have reported that person?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reported is an understatement. Had I come across such a thing, I would have personally liquidated such a person. I would have personally dealt with it. Had I come across somebody killing somebody, I would have drawn out my weapon and stopped him from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you spoke about the events of '91 and '92, and then you said that you moved to a different unit. But then you gave the date of the 1st June 2002. Was that correct? Is that the date when you were transferred to a different unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I said that but I'm sure it was a mistake in the transcript. In 1992, after my service in Vukovar, on the 1st June 1992, I moved to the anti-sabotage unit. Its tasks are well known. And then in 2002 I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what was recorded in the transcript that you moved to a different unit on the 1st of June, 1992, was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My learned friend put a lot of questions to you about your relationship with your commander and how much faith you had in him. You were saying how, at the time when you were with him, he used to tell the truth to everyone. But if I were to tell you that he stated here that he went to Ovcara on the 20th --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. I object. We're outside the scope of the cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can't see that proposition, Mr. Weiner, but I can see difficulty with the way this question is shaping. So on a different basis from what Mr. Weiner is putting, Mr. Domazet, I don't think that's a proper form of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honour. No problem whatsoever. I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke earlier about what you would have done had you learned of somebody committing a crime or misconducting, do you know that that reaction was typical for everyone in your unit, all the way up to Commander Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. That's outside the scope of cross-examination. Now he's asking to clarify an answer that he received on an issue raised in redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps more to the point, Mr. Domazet, you are clearly asking this witness to conject, because he cannot know what everyone else in his unit, or even what his commanding -- the commanding officer of his brigade, would personally have thought about those situations. It's just beyond his possible knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I meant not just him personally. But I have a couple of questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say you did not take part in any evacuations or anything like that. Do you know about the day of the fall of Vukovar? Did any of your colleagues, perhaps, help the civilian population in any way on that day?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had this professional person, Stevo Bisic, he was our logistics man. He wasn't at the front line all the time. He was our driver. He may have taken part in something. I suppose some people were involved, but I didn't specifically see anything like that, simply because I was not in all those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes and I can't say no, since ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You've said it yourself, you've answered my questions and my learned friend's questions, you don't have a very good head for dates. That is a fact. You don't even try. That's why I didn't even press you on dates. However, the day of the fall of Vukovar, you said that was important, because on that day, a day you described thoroughly today, the only time you went to Ovcara occurred on that day; right, with your unit?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking under oath here --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that. That's a speech that's leading. That's not redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the effect of it, I've been trying to find what the ultimate harm is, and the ultimate harm -- the ultimate point of the question is: Was there something significant about the day of the fall of Vukovar which imprinted that on your memory, making it different from any other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's the proper question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner, but I think that's the effect of what was being asked. In that sense, go ahead, Mr. Domazet. Do you have an answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm repeating this. This day remains etched in my memory because that was the end of the war. No more killing. No more daily danger. Will I survive? Will I not survive? So that's why that day remains etched in my memory. Later, all these dates, they just passed me by. I no longer cared. I was just looking to get out. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My last question -- my last question: Since Ovcara was brought up, if anyone were to say to you that your unit was there on a different day and not the day of the fall of Vukovar, would they be telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: RAZVIGOR VIRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that person would not be telling the truth and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object and I move to strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Will they be telling the truth? You're asking one person to comment on the credibility of another person. Can they be wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I reformulate the question, Mr. Weiner, just to make you happy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it possible that the events you've described at Ovcara could have occurred on some other date than the 18th of November, which you've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never did I mention the 18th. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's very observant of you. You're correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This occurred on the day Vukovar fell. I know how hard I found it when I settled down to be told by my commander, "Let's go, let's move on." That's one thing that stays with me, etched in my memory, this one reaction. I had already been telling myself, the war is over, it's all over, and suddenly I was called up by someone and being told to go somewhere. So it's a natural reaction. So this is something I remember in a particularly vivid way. And I certainly never mentioned the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can I re-cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're ready, Mr. Vasic, are we for another witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll be quick. Unfortunately the news is all bad today. The Victims and Witnesses Unit has informed us that, although our witnesses do have all the required visas, it just wasn't possible to get them on that plane today. Despite us being adamant that they should be arriving today, we have just received information to indicate that our two witnesses will be arriving tomorrow and another two witnesses on Saturday. This is getting up to pace now. We are processing nine witnesses. They've all been granted visas, and it's just a technical matter of having them sent over. It's about flights and about delayed flights. Unfortunately, with all the apologies due, that is the best I can say for the time being. This is not something that depends on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that last comment cannot go unnoticed. This should have been done weeks ago by you, the Defence. We must adjourn now until Friday, at 9 a.m., for the obvious reason indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.49 p.m.,
